title: Why Don't Teachers Check Prior Knowledge More Often?
author: Adam Robbins
summary: Adam Robbins identifies four reasons teachers routinely fail to explicitly check prior knowledge before teaching new content: perceived time pressure, underestimating its importance, fear of denting student confidence, and simply overestimating what students already know. Using a worked science example, he argues each barrier is weaker than it looks -- checking prior knowledge actually saves time overall, evidence on pre-testing suggests even unsuccessful attempts prime students for the material ahead, and human overconfidence about others' understanding is well-documented via confirmation bias. He closes with implementation advice: plan backwards from the lesson to identify needed prior knowledge, frame questions to elicit swift and informative answers, let teacher curiosity drive which questions to ask, and build self-correction cues into planning.
points: Robbins identifies four barriers to prior-knowledge checking: time pressure, underestimating its importance, fear of denting confidence, and teachers overestimating what students already know.

He argues checking prior knowledge actually saves time overall, since it lets teachers begin explanations further along and makes explanations more effective through priming, even though it risks 'opening a can of worms.'

Citing evidence on pre-testing, he argues even unsuccessful attempts at answering prior-knowledge questions prime students to better assimilate the coming material, reducing the risk that checking damages confidence.

His implementation advice includes planning backwards from a lesson to identify genuinely necessary prior knowledge, and using a self-correction cue: when teachers catch themselves saying 'remember when,' that's the moment to actually check.
quotes: I think checking prior knowledge is a really important part of teaching any new concept. I also think it is often overlooked.

It can save time by allowing the teacher to begin their explanation further along the narrative if the students have strong prior knowledge and it can save time crucially because the explanation will be more effective due to the priming of the relevant information.
This suggests that even if the students are unsuccessful the quizzing will identify the key information needed and prime them to assimilate it more successfully.
Humans are poor judges of other peoples understanding and experience. Think of all the cognitive biases that can hinder this, from confirmation bias to expertise blindness.
When teachers find themselves saying 'remember when' tell them that is the time to initiate the check for prior knowledge.
